# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](../packs/) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **When there's nothing left to do, say so boldly at the end of the conversation.** Don't bury a "this is complete / I'm blocked / nothing further to do" behind hedging — make the terminal state unmistakable. **Set it apart visually so it catches the eye:** put the terminal state — or, when work remains, the list of open/outstanding items — in its own callout (a Markdown blockquote box, e.g. `> ✅ All done` or `> ⚠️ Still open: …`), not trailing prose the owner has to scan for. One or the other always gets the box: the done-signal when nothing remains, the open-items list when something does.
- **"LGTM"** is the owner's phrase for the merge-to-main command: it asks for the change in front of the owner to be merged into `main`. It's an owner-triggered command; the default mechanics live in the `merge-to-main` skill ([../packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/SKILL.md](../packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/SKILL.md)) (squash, gate on CI only when the repo has it), and a project that diverges overrides them via a bespoke merge-policy file it names in its own `CLAUDE.md`.
- **"bump version"** is the owner's phrase for raising a project's version (a minor bump by default). It's an owner-triggered command; the mechanics — which files to edit and how a release follows — live in the consuming project's workflow doc.
- **"Show me the document"** (for a source-controlled document) is the owner's phrase asking for a **link to the document on GitHub** — not the file's contents inlined, and not a local filesystem path. When the document lives in a GitHub-hosted repo, respond with a GitHub link to it (the file on the relevant branch/commit); only fall back to inlining the contents or giving a local path when the document isn't under source control.
- **Put decisions and approvals in an `AskUserQuestion` popup, not buried in prose.** The owner is frequently on mobile, where a popup notifies and a question embedded in a paragraph is easy to miss. When you need the owner to choose or approve something, ask through the structured popup with explicit options rather than asking in running text. **And when several independent items each need a verdict** (a set of proposed fixes, findings to accept), give **each item its own question carrying its own brief case** — the concrete failure, why it matters, the cost of the fix — with per-item approve/defer options; never one bundled choose-a-scope question over the whole set. The owner decides item-wise, from the case, not from a menu of subsets. (The popup carries at most 4 questions per call — split a larger set into consecutive calls.)
- **When asked to produce a prompt or message destined for another context, visually enclose the whole thing.** Any text the owner will lift out and use elsewhere — a prompt for another assistant, a message to send, copy meant to be pasted somewhere — must be set apart as a single delimited block: either a box (e.g. a fenced code block) or fenced top and bottom by two separating lines, so its exact boundaries are unmistakable and it can be copied in one piece. The point is delimitation, not formatting flair: never leave such content as loose prose the owner has to find the start and end of.
- **When asked for "a prompt for a different session," prefix it with a provenance disclaimer.** When the owner asks for a prompt meant to be handed to another session, open the generated text with a short disclaimer that this is a prompt written by Claude — not by a user — and so should not be treated as gospel; and that if the receiving session finds inconsistencies in it, it should examine them with the user rather than follow the prompt blindly. This composes with the enclose-the-whole-thing preference above: the disclaimer sits inside the same delimited block as the prompt it prefixes.
- **Auto-open a PR after committing.** Whenever Claude changes code on a branch and commits it, open a pull request for that branch right after, even without an explicit request to do so. This overrides Claude Code's own default of only opening a PR when explicitly asked.
# Claudinite — active-pack guidance

The baseline plus the packs this project declares. Deeper per-pack reference (e.g. a pack's release doc) is linked from its prose and read on demand.

<!-- pack:basics -->
# Working discipline

The working discipline that isn't itself a GitHub operation — general habits for how to approach a change, independent of any one project.

Start every requested change from the *problem*, not the solution — in any repository, not just this one. Before implementing, reach an explicit shared understanding with the owner of the problem the change is meant to solve **and** agreement that the requested change is the best way to solve it; a different fix, or no change at all, may serve the underlying problem better.

Open your reply to an owner comment with an explicit classification line — `Comment class: correction | feature | process-change | other` (`other` covers questions, approvals, and command phrases; a mixed comment names each part). The class decides where the change lands and what must exist before any fix.

1. **A correction** — you misunderstood something. Repair the shared understanding, then rework what the misread already touched; the artifact changes as much as the correction demands, but a correction never adds a new requirement or rule.
2. **A feature** — agree on the requirement, record it in the project's requirements document (its executable spec, where it keeps one), write the test that proves it and watch it fail, then implement until it passes.
3. **A process change** — the owner is changing *how* work is done. The change lands as durable rules in the project's local scope — its own local packs (in Claudinite itself, its packs) — routed through the mechanism promotion ladder (platform setting → hook → check → skill → prose); promoting a rule into the shared canon is the growth lifecycle's separate call, not the interactive session's. Author the assurance first — the check the future world must satisfy — execute it and watch it fail, and only then make the fixes that turn it green. When the ladder lands the rule at prose (an in-flight judgment rule no check can carry), the equivalent step is showing the corpus doesn't already cover the rule before writing it.

The two build modes share one spine: state the expectation in its durable home first, watch it fail against the current world, then change the world to satisfy it — a fix made before its assurance exists can never show it addressed what the owner actually asked for.

Before building a mechanism for a behavior, verify against a real run that it isn't already provided.

When feedback flags a misunderstanding, check whether the artifact is already correct before expanding it — if it is, say so and push back rather than editing; a misread doesn't imply the text is wrong. And size writing to its idea: "open one issue" takes a sentence, not three paragraphs.

When correcting or auditing an artifact against an authoritative source, derive the corrected version from the *source* before reading the existing draft, then diff against the old draft to surface what was actually wrong — reading the draft first anchors you to its framing and quietly carries its errors into your "fix."

Fix build/test/CI warnings rather than tolerating them, with a small, targeted fix that addresses the *cause* in the same change — a clean run makes a genuinely new warning or error stand out.

Suppressing a warning — muting it with a flag (e.g. `--disable-warning`), `eslint-disable`, swallowing it, etc. — is **not** a small fix and never the quick path: reach for it only as a deliberate, reviewed decision once the real fix has been weighed and rejected. A suppression you do keep must **carry its reason at the site**: on the suppression line, or in the comment immediately above it, saying why the fix was rejected — that inline reason *is* the review record, so no second justification is recorded elsewhere.

Before working around a finding from a vendored check, confirm the vendored copy is current — it reflects its last refresh, not upstream's head, so the fix may already exist upstream and simply not be pulled in yet.

When a warning can't be fixed with a small cause-addressing change now without hindering current work (e.g. it's waiting on an upstream release, or the real fix is a larger refactor), open a dedicated issue for it unless one is already open, then move on — resolving it (real fix, or a consciously-chosen suppression) happens in that issue's own change.

An approval — to merge, to ship, to proceed — applies only *backward*, to the work already in front of the owner when it's given, never to anything requested or done *after* it. A later follow-up, even a fix to the just-approved change, needs its own explicit approval; a chosen answer to a multiple-choice prompt isn't authorization just because an option's wording mentioned the action.

# The task lifecycle

The issue → branch → PR lifecycle every new task follows, independent of any one project. The rest of the git/GitHub procedures live in the `git-github-advanced` skill.

For every new task:

1. Create a GitHub issue describing the task before starting work.
2. Develop on a branch; reference that issue number in commit messages (e.g. `Refs #123`, `Fixes #123`, or `Closes #123`).
3. Update the issue's status (comments / close) as work progresses and when it's done.

---

<!-- pack:tidy-repo -->
# tidy-repo — the repo tidy-up policy

The PR/branch/issue sweep, active wherever this pack is declared. The repo's own scheduler runs the
pack's three maintenance tasks — `tidy-issues`, `tidy-prs`, `tidy-branches`, one per dimension; this is
the policy they follow. The per-object **method** lives in the pack's skills
([single-branch-status](skills/single-branch-status/SKILL.md),
[single-pr-status](skills/single-pr-status/SKILL.md),
[single-issue-triage](skills/single-issue-triage/SKILL.md)).

The one rule that shapes everything: **assess PRs and branches read-only; act only on issues.**

- **Branches, PRs — assess only.** Report which should stay and which are safe to close/delete;
  **never** delete, push, merge, or close them. Judge by *content* (the landed-status test), never a
  ref's auto-generated name.
- **Issues — act.** Take the first applicable action: close-if-implemented / needs-decision / blocked
  / quick-win / leave. "Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s
  content **now** — confirm it there and cite it; when you can't, comment, don't close. Every action
  defaults to the reversible option (comment / leave) when the check is inconclusive.

Each task applies its single-object skill across the targets its precondition hands it, then rewrites
**its own** standing tracker from the verdicts it gathered (one issue per dimension per repo, body
rewritten to today's state, a dated comment per run). One tracker per task, never a shared one: the
three tasks are independent and may run at once, so nothing races to rewrite one body.

---

<!-- pack:laughcounter -->
# Working in this repo

The general lessons this repo has paid for once. The privacy boundary — the
product's defining constraint — has its own pack (`local/on-device-privacy`);
what follows is everything else.

**Don't prune a `.gitignore` section in the same breath as deleting what it
ignored — the artifacts are still on disk.** Removing a toolchain (the Python
reference, a build system, a generator) invites tidying its ignore rules away in
the same commit, but the ignored artifacts it already produced are usually still
sitting untracked in the worktree — earlier test runs leave `__pycache__/`,
builds leave `build/`. The moment those rules go, the next `git add -A` sweeps
the artifacts *into* the very commit that was supposed to remove them, and
nothing complains: the commit is valid, the tests still pass, and the junk only
shows up as an inflated file count in the diff a reviewer reads. Delete the
artifacts from the worktree first (or `git clean` them), then drop their ignore
lines — and read `git diff --cached --stat` after any bulk `git add -A`, not just
`git status`, since staged additions are exactly what a clean `git status` stops
telling you about.

---

<!-- pack:on-device-privacy -->
# On-device privacy — the boundary the whole product is built around

An always-on microphone in someone's living room only earns its place if what it
hears stays on the machine. That promise is the product requirement
(`docs/DESIGN-AND-TRADEOFFS.md` §0/§6, README *Privacy*), the text of the mic and
speech prompts users actually see (`mac/Resources/Info.plist`), and the reason
several design choices look heavier than they need to. The checks in this pack
hold the mechanical half; what follows is the judgment half.

There is now exactly one implementation — the native app in `mac/Sources/` — so
every rule below is about it.

**What may cross the boundary: derived metadata, never audio.** A laugh is
persisted as time, duration, confidence, and an origin label — that is what the
JSONL lines carry, and `LaughStore` says so in its own header. **No audio is
stored at all** — the `no-audio-persistence` check holds this mechanically for
v1. A feature that wants to keep audio (the v3 roadmap's rolling buffer) is not
a new field, it is a new promise to the user: it changes the mic prompt and this
check together, in the same PR.

**Everything lives in one deletable directory.**
`~/Library/Application Support/LaughCounter/` holds the laugh log and the app's
own diagnostic log, and nothing lands outside it (the one path macOS dictates, not
us, is a Login Item registration). "Delete the folder and it's gone" is a promise a
user *acts on* — someone who deletes it believes the mic's whole memory of them
went with it. So a feature needing somewhere new to keep things extends that
directory rather than earning a second one.

**There is no accepted egress — none.** Detection (Sound Analysis) and speech
recognition (`SFSpeechRecognizer` with on-device recognition required) are both
built into macOS; no model is downloaded, no telemetry is sent, and the app makes
no outbound connection of any kind. The `no-network-client` check is therefore
absolute rather than carve-out-shaped. Adding *any* egress — a model fetch, a
crash reporter, a sync feature — is a product decision that gets written here and
in the README *Privacy* section before a line of it is written in Swift.

**There is no server either.** The app listens on no socket. The web dashboard
that once existed in the Python reference was removed on purpose, along with the
reference itself. Reintroducing any listener — a dashboard, a metrics port, a
remote-control API — is a decision about exposing the laugh log, not a feature to
slip in: it needs the owner's explicit sign-off, a loopback-only default, and a
story for authentication or CSRF before it lands.

**The disclosure must stay true.** `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription` and
`NSSpeechRecognitionUsageDescription` tell the user audio is analysed on-device
and not recorded. If the app's behaviour ever changes, those strings change with
it in the same commit — a stale privacy prompt is worse than a blunt one.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

- docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files) or Word templates (.dotx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. 12	overlap restarts. (#22)
13	
14	## Never reuse an `AVAudioEngine` across a device change (#61)
15	
16	An `AVAudioEngine` caches the input hardware format when its input node is first
17	materialized, and **the cache does not follow the device**. After CoreAudio tears
18	the input down — a USB mic re-enumerating, or coreaudiod dropping its contexts
19	when the display sleeps — `inputNode.outputFormat(forBus: 0)` still reports the
20	*old* rate, while `installTap` validates against the freshly-queried hardware
21	format. They disagree, and `installTap` raises an **uncatchable** NSException:
22	`required condition is false: format.sampleRate == inputHWFormat.sampleRate`.
23	
24	This killed the app on **every** configuration change — six for six over fifteen
25	days on the owner's Mac mini, the longest outage fifteen days of nobody noticing.
26	The pre-tap guard added in #22 did not help, because it compared the stale cache
27	against itself and always passed: not the microsecond race its comment assumed,
28	but a design gap. So `AudioHub.prepareFormat()` **builds a new engine every time**
29	(stopping the old one first — dropping the last reference to a *running* engine
30	abandons its IOProc on the device, the wedge condition). Three consequences:
31	
32	- **The crash was also the mic-wedge cause.** An uncaught NSException aborts the
33	  process, so `applicationWillTerminate` never runs and the tap's IOProc is left
34	  registered — the BRIO went dead until physically re-plugged. The exit-path rule
35	  below calls crash teardown "residual risk"; at six crashes in fifteen days it
36	  was the main risk.
37	- **A replaced engine invalidates an observer bound to the old instance**, so
38	  `AudioHub` owns the `.AVAudioEngineConfigurationChange` observation and
39	  republishes it via `onConfigurationChange` (delivered on main). Registering it
40	  from `AppDelegate` against `audio.engine` would go quiet after the first
41	  restart — and a quiet config-change observer means the app stops noticing that
42	  its microphone vanished.
43	- **Swift cannot catch `NSException`**, so the last line of defence is a few
44	  lines of Objective-C (`Sources/ObjCExceptionTrap`, its own SwiftPM target — our
45	  source, not a dependency). Catching one is only safe because these calls
46	  validate *before* mutating anything; don't wrap framework calls in general.
47	  Treat the trap as **unproven** until something demonstrates it catching a real
48	  raise: the exception has to unwind through the intervening Swift closure frame,
49	  which is not guaranteed to work.
50	
51	**A new engine must have a node attached before `prepare()`.** `AVAudioEngine`
52	initializes its graph inside `prepare()` and asserts `inputNode != nullptr ||
53	outputNode != nullptr` — another uncatchable NSException. A freshly constructed
54	engine has neither: `inputNode` is created lazily *on first access*, and touching
55	the property is what attaches it. `AudioHub.makeEngine()` does that as part of
56	building one, so no call ordering elsewhere can get it wrong. The single-engine

59	rebuilding the engine *after* that call removed the accident: v0.3.0 crashed one
60	second into every launch. (#72)

63	node, `inputFormat(forBus: 0)` is the *hardware* format — the one `installTap`
64	asserts on. `outputFormat(forBus: 0)` is the bus's output format, and with the
65	device torn down it still reports a plausible 48 kHz while `inputFormat` reports

73	~20 seconds and it does not return until the displays wake (28 minutes in one
74	measurement). Recovery arrives as an `.AVAudioEngineConfigurationChange` when the
75	device reappears. So a *bounded* retry ladder is the wrong shape — it expires
76	with the cause fully present — and the give-up message must not blame the
77	hardware. Back off to a ceiling and keep checking; a cheap format read once a
78	minute is nowhere near the rate that cycles a mic.

86	(`displaysleep 20`), and coreaudiod tears its contexts down seconds later.

91	`applicationWillTerminate` — but **NSApplication installs no signal handlers**:
92	a bare SIGTERM (Activity Monitor "Quit", `killall`), SIGINT (Ctrl-C in a dev

103	delayed engine start (the +0.4s `finishListening`, the +1.0s wake resume) that a
104	stop raced with would otherwise re-acquire the mic going *into* sleep or

106	delayed closure captures the generation at schedule time and aborts if it moved.

108	`restartQueued` / `suppressConfigChange`, or the latches stay stuck and block
109	all future starts.

114	`NSWorkspace.didWakeNotification` is all you get, and it is **not equivalent to "the
115	machine is back"** — a dark/Power-Nap wake fires it with nobody there and the Mac
116	re-sleeps moments later. So `systemDidReturn(reason:)` fans in four signals —
117	`didWake`, `screensDidWake`, `sessionDidBecomeActive`, and the distributed
118	`com.apple.screenIsUnlocked` — and coalesces them, because a real return fires

126	  or double-scheduling.

128	  Displays wake and sessions activate with no sleep involved (screensaver, user
129	  switching); reacting to those would cycle a healthy engine — the wedge condition.
130	- **Always ungate `sleeping` in the resume timer**, even on the "stay off" path, or
131	  `requestListening` stays blocked forever and the menu's Start item does nothing.
132	- The distributed unlock notification is free here because the app is
133	  non–App Store (no App Sandbox). Under the sandbox it silently never arrives; the
134	  three workspace triggers still cover the case.
135

137	
138	`listening` ("the engine is running") is not the state a wake should branch on.
139	`listeningIntent` ("the counter is meant to be running") is: sleep suspends capture
140	without clearing it, so a return reactivates only a counter that was actually
141	active, while a start that merely *failed* keeps it and stays eligible for recovery.
142	Branching on `listening` instead would make any pre-sleep failure permanent.
143

145	`listeningIntent` is derived from it — rather than a bool beside a separate reason
146	string. The menu status, the tooltip and the wake log all render that one field, so

148	"no microphone access", "starting up"). Menu **Pause listening** sets it; every
149	request to listen clears it, which is what asking to listen means.
150

152	re-enumerating when the settle window closes. That start throws, and — unlike the
153	config-change cases — **nothing else will ever fire** to recover from it, so the app
154	sits silently "not listening" until someone opens the menu. Hence
155	`scheduleStartRetry`: doubling 2s → 32s, capped at `maxStartRetries`, reset on every

159	lasted longer than `standbyThreshold`; measure that span with `Date()`, **not**
160	`ProcessInfo.systemUptime`, which does not advance while the machine is asleep.
161	
162	## Config-change suppression must reconcile, not just drop
163	
164	CoreAudio posts `.AVAudioEngineConfigurationChange` for our *own* stop/start
165	(react → infinite restart loop, hence the suppress window) **and** for genuine
166	device events — including while the machine heads into sleep (hence the
167	`sleeping` gate from `willSleep` until the post-wake settle). A genuine event

176	  running and it releases what `prepare()` allocated — a prepare-then-throw
177	  path would otherwise keep the input unit holding the device.
178	- `installTap` with a format the hardware no longer matches raises an
179	  **uncatchable NSException** — re-validate the live format immediately before
180	  the tap (narrows, doesn't eliminate; there is no atomic API).
181	- `SFSpeechRecognizer` fed via `SFSpeechAudioBufferRecognitionRequest` never

183	  main, the Speech callback queue, *and* the audio tap thread: everything in

185	  task store on *request identity* (`request === newRequest`), because a
186	  restart() between the phases leaves `running == true` — gating on `running`
187	  would store a dead task and permanently block the idempotency guard.

# LaughCounter — local project procedures

Project-specific instructions for this repo, layered on the shared Claudinite
canon (vendored into the repo, read-only). Where a local rule refines a canon
rule, the local one wins — it carries this project's concrete files and gotchas.
Routing index, not a payload: read the matching doc when its trigger fires; don't
pre-load.

Capture lessons **here, locally**, in the doc that owns the topic. A lesson's
*portability* is Claudinite's concern (its growth routine lifts portable lessons
up into the shared canon) — not a reason to capture it anywhere else.

- [ci-release.md](ci-release.md) — **before touching the release/CI workflows
  (`.github/workflows/*-macos-dmg.yml`).** How the DMG gets published to GitHub
  Releases, and the trigger gotchas learned wiring it up.
- [mac-audio-lifecycle.md](mac-audio-lifecycle.md) — **before touching engine
  start/stop, sleep/wake, exit handling, or `VoiceCommand` in
  `mac/Sources/LaughCounter/`.** The release-the-mic-on-every-path invariant
  (USB webcam mics wedge otherwise), signal routing, generation-guarded deferred
  work, and config-change reconciliation.

@ci-release.md

# CI & release — the macOS DMG

How `LaughCounter.dmg` reaches users, and the workflow-trigger gotchas learned
wiring it up. Read before editing `.github/workflows/release-macos-dmg.yml` or
`build-macos-dmg.yml`.

**The shape.** `release-macos-dmg.yml` owns `main`: on a push to `main` touching
`mac/**` it builds the DMG, derives `v<version>` from `mac/Resources/Info.plist`,
and creates/updates that GitHub Release with `LaughCounter.dmg` attached — so the
README's stable `releases/latest/download/LaughCounter.dmg` link always resolves.
`build-macos-dmg.yml` is the feature-branch artifact builder and **excludes
`main`** (`branches: ["**", "!main"]`) so it never duplicates the release build.

## Trigger the release on push-to-main, not a `v*` tag push

A Claude Code **web session pushes through a git-only proxy that cannot push
`v*` tags**, so a release workflow keyed on `push: tags` never fires from a
session — the Release area stays empty and the `latest/download` link 404s. Key
the release on **push to `main`** (scoped to `mac/**`) instead: the job derives
`v<version>` from `Info.plist` and creates the tag + Release with `GITHUB_TOKEN`,
which *can* tag and release from within Actions even though the session can't.
(#18 / #19)

## A UI-published Release does not fire `push: tags` — add `release: published`

Publishing a Release from the GitHub UI creates the tag but does **not** emit a
`push: tags` event, so a workflow listening only for tag pushes won't build for
it. Keep a `release: types: [published]` trigger alongside the push-to-main one so
a hand-published Release still builds and attaches the DMG. (#11 / #13)

## Why the two triggers don't loop or double-build

- The tag + Release the push-to-main job creates is made with `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and
  a Release created by `GITHUB_TOKEN` does **not** re-fire the `release` event —
  so the `release: published` trigger doesn't re-run it. (This is the canon's
  general "`GITHUB_TOKEN` doesn't start another workflow" rule, applied to the
  `release` event specifically.)
- `build-macos-dmg.yml` excludes `main`, so a `mac/**` push to `main` builds once
  (in the release job), not twice.

## Signing & notarization is an optional, secret-gated lane (#4)

Both DMG workflows have an **optional** Developer ID signing + Apple notarization
lane that runs only when the signing secrets are set (`MACOS_CERT_P12`,
`MACOS_CERT_PASSWORD`, `MACOS_SIGN_IDENTITY`, `APPLE_ID`, `APPLE_TEAM_ID`,
`APPLE_APP_PASSWORD`); without them the build still passes and ships an **ad-hoc**
DMG. **Keep it secret-gated** — never make signing a required step, or a fork or
secret-less build breaks. The signing/notarization how-to and the user-facing
Gatekeeper steps live in `mac/README.md`; `scripts/build-app.sh` signs and
`scripts/notarize-dmg.sh` notarizes + staples. The CI-side gotchas that aren't in
the README:

- **Notarization requires the Hardened Runtime** (`codesign --options runtime`),
  and under it the mic needs an explicit entitlement
  (`com.apple.security.device.audio-input`, in
  `mac/Resources/LaughCounter.entitlements`) that an ad-hoc build doesn't — so
  turning on notarization silently kills mic access unless the entitlement ships
  with it. (Speech recognition is gated by TCC + the Info.plist usage string, not
  a codesign entitlement, so it needs nothing there.)
- **An ad-hoc signature can't be notarized** — they're separate lanes; only the
  Developer-ID-signed `.app` (built when `MACOS_SIGN_IDENTITY` is set) can be
  submitted to the notary service.
- **The ephemeral signing keychain must be added to the searchable keychain
  list** (`security list-keychains -d user -s "$KEYCHAIN" $(security
  list-keychains -d user | sed …)`) or `codesign` can't find the imported
  identity. That `sed` pipe is why the workflows set `defaults.run.shell: bash`
  for pipefail (#27; enforced by the canon `gha/run-pipefail` check).
- **macOS 15 (Sequoia) removed the right-click → Open Gatekeeper bypass** — the
  ad-hoc install path is now System Settings → Privacy & Security → *Open Anyway*,
  or `xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine <app>` (see `mac/README.md`).
- This is the **non–App Store** track (no App Sandbox); a Mac App Store build
  would need the App Sandbox and a different Apple Distribution certificate.

2	import ObjCExceptionTrap

4	/// Owns the microphone. A single input tap fans each captured buffer out to
5	/// every consumer (the laughter detector *and* the speech recogniser), so the
6	/// two never fight over the input node.
7	///
8	/// The `AVAudioEngine` is **rebuilt on every start** rather than held for the
9	/// process lifetime — see `prepareFormat()` for why that is load-bearing and not
10	/// tidiness. Because the engine instance changes, this class also owns the
11	/// `.AVAudioEngineConfigurationChange` observation and republishes it through
12	/// `onConfigurationChange`: an observer registered against a replaced engine goes
13	/// quiet, and a quiet config-change observer means the app stops noticing that
14	/// its microphone disappeared.
15	final class AudioHub {
16	    private var engine: AVAudioEngine
17	    private var configObserver: NSObjectProtocol?
18	
19	    /// Called for every captured buffer, on the audio thread.
20	    var onBuffer: ((AVAudioPCMBuffer, AVAudioTime) -> Void)?
21	
22	    /// Called on the main queue when CoreAudio reports that the current engine's
23	    /// configuration changed (device added, removed, or switched under us).
24	    var onConfigurationChange: (() -> Void)?
25	
26	    /// The input format currently in use (valid only once `start(format:)` ran).
27	    private(set) var activeFormat: AVAudioFormat?
28	
29	    var isRunning: Bool { engine.isRunning }
30	
31	    init() {
32	        engine = Self.makeEngine()
33	        observeConfigurationChange()
34	    }
35	
36	    /// Build an engine that is safe to `prepare()`.
37	    ///
38	    /// `AVAudioEngine` initializes its graph inside `prepare()` and asserts that
39	    /// at least one node is attached — `inputNode != nullptr || outputNode !=
40	    /// nullptr` — raising an uncatchable NSException when none is. A freshly
41	    /// constructed engine has none: `inputNode` is created lazily *on first
42	    /// access*, and touching the property is what attaches it. So materialize it
43	    /// here, as part of building an engine, rather than leaving it to a call
44	    /// order somewhere else.
45	    ///
46	    /// The pre-rebuild code survived only by accident: `requestListening()` calls
47	    /// `stop()`, which reaches `engine.inputNode.removeTap(onBus: 0)` and
48	    /// materialized the node on the single long-lived engine long before any
49	    /// `prepare()`. Rebuilding the engine after that call removed the accident,
50	    /// and every launch crashed one second in. (#72)
51	    private static func makeEngine() -> AVAudioEngine {
52	        let engine = AVAudioEngine()
53	        _ = engine.inputNode   // attaches it; do not "simplify" this away
54	        return engine
55	    }
56	
57	    deinit {
58	        if let observer = configObserver {
59	            NotificationCenter.default.removeObserver(observer)
60	        }
61	    }
62	
63	    /// Build a fresh engine and return its validated live input format, **without**
64	    /// starting capture. The input node's format is only reliable after prepare;
65	    /// returning it first lets the detector be configured to match *before* any
66	    /// audio flows (the analyzer must exist before buffers arrive, or the first
67	    /// buffers are dropped and analysis can fail to start).
68	    ///
69	    /// The engine is replaced here rather than reused, and that is the fix for
70	    /// #61. An `AVAudioEngine` caches the input hardware format when its input
71	    /// node is first materialized, and the cache does not follow the device: after
72	    /// CoreAudio tears the input down — a USB mic re-enumerating, or coreaudiod
73	    /// dropping its contexts when the display sleeps — `inputNode.outputFormat(
74	    /// forBus: 0)` keeps reporting the *old* rate. `installTap` validates against
75	    /// the freshly-queried hardware format instead, the two disagree, and it
76	    /// raises an uncatchable NSException. That killed the app on every single
77	    /// configuration change (six for six over fifteen days) — not the rare race
78	    /// the previous guard assumed, because comparing the stale cache against
79	    /// itself always passed. A new engine reads the hardware fresh, so the guard
80	    /// in `start(format:)` is meaningful again and the two formats agree.
81	    func prepareFormat() throws -> AVAudioFormat {
82	        renewEngine()
83	        // Trapped as well as installTap: #59 wrapped only the tap install, and
84	        // prepare() then raised from a path with no trap in it at all. Anything
85	        // that can raise on the way to capture gets the same treatment. (#72)
86	        try ObjCExceptionTrap.run { engine.prepare() }
87	        return try validatedFormat()
88	    }
89	
90	    /// The tap format, checked against the *hardware* format that `installTap`
91	    /// asserts on.
92	    ///
93	    /// Read `inputFormat(forBus: 0)`, not `outputFormat`: `outputFormat` is the
94	    /// bus's output format, and with the input device torn down it still reports
95	    /// a plausible 48 kHz while `inputFormat` correctly reports 0. Checking
96	    /// `outputFormat` therefore could not detect an absent microphone at all — it
97	    /// waved through starts that could never succeed and left `installTap` to
98	    /// raise, which is what the exception trap kept catching once a minute while
99	    /// the displays slept. Requiring the two to agree means `installTap` is never
100	    /// reached in the mismatch state. (#76)
101	    private func validatedFormat() throws -> AVAudioFormat {
102	        let input = engine.inputNode
103	        let hardware = input.inputFormat(forBus: 0)
104	        let bus = input.outputFormat(forBus: 0)
105	        guard hardware.sampleRate > 0, hardware.channelCount > 0 else {
106	            throw NSError(domain: "LaughCounter", code: 1, userInfo: [
107	                NSLocalizedDescriptionKey:
108	                    "no input hardware — the microphone is not available "
109	                    + "(sampleRate=\(hardware.sampleRate), channels=\(hardware.channelCount))",
110	            ])
111	        }
112	        guard hardware.sampleRate == bus.sampleRate,
113	              hardware.channelCount == bus.channelCount else {
114	            throw NSError(domain: "LaughCounter", code: 2, userInfo: [
115	                NSLocalizedDescriptionKey:
116	                    "input format unsettled "
117	                    + "(hardware \(hardware.sampleRate)Hz/\(hardware.channelCount)ch, "
118	                    + "bus \(bus.sampleRate)Hz/\(bus.channelCount)ch)",
119	            ])
120	        }
121	        return bus
122	    }
123	
124	    /// Install the tap and start capture, using a format from `prepareFormat()`.
125	    func start(format: AVAudioFormat) throws {
126	        let input = engine.inputNode
127	        // Re-validate against the hardware immediately before the tap: the device
128	        // can still vanish between prepareFormat() and here (dock unplug,
129	        // wake-time re-enumeration), and a mismatch reaching installTap is what
130	        // raises. Checking the same pair as prepareFormat did, because the bus
131	        // format alone cannot tell an absent device from a present one. (#76)
132	        let live = try validatedFormat()
133	        guard live.sampleRate == format.sampleRate,
134	              live.channelCount == format.channelCount else {
135	            throw NSError(domain: "LaughCounter", code: 3, userInfo: [
136	                NSLocalizedDescriptionKey:
137	                    "input device changed between prepare and start "
138	                    + "(expected \(format.sampleRate)Hz/\(format.channelCount)ch, "
139	                    + "live \(live.sampleRate)Hz/\(live.channelCount)ch)",
140	            ])
141	        }
142	        input.removeTap(onBus: 0)   // no-op if none installed; keeps restart clean
143	        // Backstop: installTap raises an *uncatchable* NSException if its format
144	        // disagrees with the live hardware, and Swift cannot catch one — it aborts
145	        // the process, skipping the tap teardown in applicationWillTerminate and
146	        // leaving the IOProc registered, which is exactly what wedges a USB webcam
147	        // mic until it is physically re-plugged. This is not theoretical and not
148	        // dead code: it demonstrably caught that exception once a minute while the
149	        // displays slept, which is the only reason the app survived. The guard
150	        // above should now keep us off that path; this stays because there is no
151	        // atomic API and being wrong here costs the microphone.
152	        try ObjCExceptionTrap.run {
153	            input.installTap(onBus: 0, bufferSize: 8192, format: format) { [weak self] buffer, when in
154	                self?.onBuffer?(buffer, when)
155	            }
156	        }
157	        try engine.start()
158	        activeFormat = format
159	    }
160	
161	    func stop() {
162	        engine.inputNode.removeTap(onBus: 0)
163	        // Unconditional: engine.stop() is safe on a non-running engine, and it also
164	        // releases what engine.prepare() allocated — a prepare()-then-throw path
165	        // (prepareFormat/configure failing before start) would otherwise leave the
166	        // initialized input unit holding the device.
167	        engine.stop()
168	        activeFormat = nil
169	    }
170	
171	    /// Tear the current engine down and put a fresh one in its place. Stopping
172	    /// first is what keeps the release-the-mic invariant: dropping the last
173	    /// reference to a *running* engine would abandon its tap and IOProc on the
174	    /// device instead of deregistering them.
175	    private func renewEngine() {
176	        stop()
177	        engine = Self.makeEngine()
178	        observeConfigurationChange()
179	    }
180	
181	    /// (Re)point the configuration-change observation at the current engine.
182	    private func observeConfigurationChange() {
183	        if let observer = configObserver {
184	            NotificationCenter.default.removeObserver(observer)
185	        }
186	        // Delivered on the main queue so the callback can touch app state directly;
187	        // CoreAudio posts this from whatever thread noticed the change.
188	        configObserver = NotificationCenter.default.addObserver(
189	            forName: .AVAudioEngineConfigurationChange, object: engine, queue: .main
190	        ) { [weak self] _ in
191	            self?.onConfigurationChange?()
192	        }
193	    }
194	}

167	    /// Tears down, lets the input device settle briefly, then re-acquires.
168	    private func requestListening() {
169	        guard micGranted else { return }
170	        // Record the intent before the sleep gate, so a manual "Start listening"
171	        // clicked during a sleep transition is still honored by the resume — and
172	        // so it clears a pause, which is what asking to listen means.
173	        offReason = nil
174	        if sleeping {                  // heading into (or settling out of) sleep:
175	            // the post-wake resume is the one path out; log so a swallowed manual
176	            // click is visible in the activity log rather than silently ignored
177	            AppLog.shared.log("listening request ignored (sleep transition in progress)")
178	            return
179	        }
180	        if restartInFlight {           // coalesce; don't stack restarts
181	            restartQueued = true
182	            return
183	        }
184	        restartInFlight = true
185	        suppressConfigChange = true    // ignore the config-changes our stop/start emits
186	        configChangeSwallowed = false  // fresh window; note only events from this cycle
187	        restartGeneration &+= 1
188	        let generation = restartGeneration
189	        counter.flush()
190	        counter.reset()
191	        detector.reset()
192	        audio.stop()
193	        listening = false
194	        refreshTitle()
195	        // Let the (USB) input device release before re-acquiring — reacquiring
196	        // immediately after teardown is what can wedge some USB mics.
197	        DispatchQueue.main.asyncAfter(deadline: .now() + 0.4) { [weak self] in
198	            self?.finishListening(generation: generation)
199	        }
200	    }
201	
202	    private func finishListening(generation: Int) {
203	        // A stop (sleep/terminate) superseded this restart while it waited — the
204	        // mic must stay released, not be re-acquired behind the stop's back.
205	        guard generation == restartGeneration else { return }
206	        do {
207	            // Configure the analyzer BEFORE audio flows, so no early buffers are
208	            // dropped and analysis reliably starts (matches the original order).
209	            let format = try audio.prepareFormat()
210	            try detector.configure(format: format)
211	            try audio.start(format: format)
212	            listening = true
213	            startFailureStreak = 0
214	            AppLog.shared.log("listening started "
215	                + "(sampleRate=\(Int(format.sampleRate)), channels=\(format.channelCount))")
216	        } catch {
217	            audio.stop()
218	            listening = false
219	            startFailureStreak += 1
220	            AppLog.shared.log("could not start listening: \(error.localizedDescription)",
221	                              level: "ERROR")
222	        }
223	        refreshTitle()
224	        buildMenu()
225	        // Settle window: no further restart (or config-change reaction) until the
226	        // engine has run undisturbed for a moment. Then honor any coalesced request.
227	        DispatchQueue.main.asyncAfter(deadline: .now() + 1.2) { [weak self] in
228	            guard let self = self, generation == self.restartGeneration else { return }
229	            self.suppressConfigChange = false
230	            self.restartInFlight = false
231	            let swallowed = self.configChangeSwallowed
232	            self.configChangeSwallowed = false
233	            if self.restartQueued {
234	                self.restartQueued = false
235	                self.requestListening()
236	            } else if self.listening && !self.audio.isRunning {
237	                // A genuine config change landed inside the suppress window and
238	                // halted the engine (AVAudioEngine stops rendering when the
239	                // device changes under it). The suppression rightly ignored the
240	                // notification — self-emitted ones would loop — so reconcile by
241	                // state instead: "listening" but engine dead means we owe a
242	                // restart, otherwise the UI claims listening while nothing flows.
243	                AppLog.shared.log("engine halted during settle — restarting", level: "WARN")
244	                self.requestListening()
245	            } else if !self.listening && swallowed {
246	                // Complementary case: this cycle's start FAILED (no device yet),
247	                // and the device's arrival notification landed inside the window.
248	                // Dropping it would leave the app "not listening" with no further
249	                // event to recover on. One retry per swallowed event — a dead mic
250	                // emits no events, so this can't poll forever.
251	                AppLog.shared.log("device event during settle after failed start — retrying")
252	                self.requestListening()
253	            } else if !self.listening && self.listeningIntent {
254	                // The counter is meant to be on but the start failed and no device
255	                // event arrived to hang a retry off. The reachable case is a return
256	                // from standby: the machine powered the USB bus down, so the mic is
257	                // still re-enumerating when the settle window ends and there is
258	                // nothing left to recover on — the app would sit silently "not
259	                // listening" until someone opened the menu. So back off and try
260	                // again, doubling each time (2s, 4s … 32s) and giving up after
261	                // `maxStartRetries`: bounded, because a mic that is gone for good
262	                // emits nothing and must not be polled forever, and slow, because
263	                // rapid-cycling a USB mic is what wedges it in the first place.
264	                self.scheduleStartRetry(generation: generation)
265	            }
266	        }
267	    }
268	
269	    /// Back-off retry after a failed start, generation-guarded like every other
270	    /// deferred restart: an intentional stop, or any restart accepted meanwhile,
271	    /// moves the generation and this retry aborts rather than re-acquiring the mic
272	    /// behind it. Main-thread only.
273	    private func scheduleStartRetry(generation: Int) {
274	        let attempt = startFailureStreak
275	        // Double up to the ceiling, then keep checking at that interval for as
276	        // long as the counter is meant to be on. Deliberately never gives up: the
277	        // measured cause of a long outage is the input device being torn down
278	        // while the displays sleep, which lasted 28 minutes in one observation —
279	        // no bounded ladder covers that, and the old five attempts (~62s) expired
280	        // with the cause still fully present, telling the user to reconnect a
281	        // microphone that was fine. A start attempt is now a cheap format read
282	        // that throws before touching the tap, and one a minute is far below any
283	        // rate that could cycle a USB mic. (#76)
284	        let delay = min(Double(1 << min(attempt, 6)), maxBackoffDelay)
285	        if attempt <= maxStartRetries {
286	            AppLog.shared.log("start failed — retrying in \(Int(delay))s "
287	                + "(attempt \(attempt) of \(maxStartRetries))", level: "WARN")
288	        } else if attempt == maxStartRetries + 1 {
289	            // Announce the switch to slow checking once, then stay quiet until it
290	            // works — a line a minute for half an hour buries everything else.
291	            AppLog.shared.log("input device still unavailable — checking every "
292	                + "\(Int(maxBackoffDelay))s until it returns (expected while the "
293	                + "displays are asleep; no action needed)", level: "WARN")
294	        }
295	        DispatchQueue.main.asyncAfter(deadline: .now() + delay) { [weak self] in
296	            guard let self = self, generation == self.restartGeneration else { return }
297	            guard self.listeningIntent, !self.listening else { return }
298	            self.requestListening()
299	        }
300	    }

302	    private func stopListening(reason: String) {
303	        // Invalidate the whole in-flight restart machinery, not just the queue
304	        // flag: a pending finishListening must never fire after an intentional
305	        // stop (it would re-acquire the mic right as the system sleeps), and the
306	        // in-flight/suppress latches must not stay stuck blocking future starts.
307	        restartGeneration &+= 1
308	        restartInFlight = false
309	        restartQueued = false
310	        suppressConfigChange = false
311	        pendingResumeID = nil   // a resume scheduled before this stop is void
312	        counter.flush()
313	        voice.stop()     // symmetric with resume; recognition restarts on wake
314	        audio.stop()
315	        listening = false
316	        AppLog.shared.log("listening stopped (\(reason))")
317	        refreshTitle()
318	        buildMenu()
319	    }

322	        SFSpeechRecognizer.requestAuthorization { [weak self] status in
323	            DispatchQueue.main.async {
324	                guard status == .authorized else {
325	                    AppLog.shared.log("speech recognition not authorized", level: "WARN")
326	                    return
327	                }
328	                self?.speechAuthorized = true
329	                self?.voice.start()

332	        }

335	    // MARK: system power / audio events

337	    private func observeSystemEvents() {
338	        let ws = NSWorkspace.shared.notificationCenter
339	        ws.addObserver(self, selector: #selector(willSleep),
340	                       name: NSWorkspace.willSleepNotification, object: nil)
341	        // macOS has no "returned from standby" notification — standby is just a
342	        // deeper sleep, and the only guaranteed signal is the ordinary wake. But a
343	        // wake is not always a *return*: a dark/Power-Nap wake fires it with nobody
344	        // there and the machine drops straight back to sleep, and after a long
345	        // standby the mic can still be re-enumerating when our settle window ends.
346	        // So take the wake plus every other "the machine is back" signal and funnel
347	        // them into one coalesced resume; whichever lands first schedules it, the
348	        // later ones act as backstops if that resume didn't get the counter running.
349	        ws.addObserver(self, selector: #selector(didWake),
350	                       name: NSWorkspace.didWakeNotification, object: nil)
351	        ws.addObserver(self, selector: #selector(screensDidWake),
352	                       name: NSWorkspace.screensDidWakeNotification, object: nil)
353	        ws.addObserver(self, selector: #selector(sessionDidBecomeActive),
354	                       name: NSWorkspace.sessionDidBecomeActiveNotification, object: nil)
355	        // Unlocking after standby is the strongest "a person is actually back"
356	        // signal, but it only exists as a *distributed* notification. That is fine
357	        // for this app (non–App Store, no App Sandbox); under the sandbox it would
358	        // simply never arrive, and the workspace triggers above still cover us.
359	        DistributedNotificationCenter.default().addObserver(
360	            self, selector: #selector(screenDidUnlock),
361	            name: NSNotification.Name("com.apple.screenIsUnlocked"), object: nil)
362	        // AudioHub owns the .AVAudioEngineConfigurationChange observation because
363	        // it replaces the engine on every start (#61) and an observer bound to a
364	        // superseded instance would silently stop firing. It delivers on main.
365	        audio.onConfigurationChange = { [weak self] in self?.audioConfigChanged() }
366	    }

368	    @objc private func willSleep() {
369	        // Gate BEFORE tearing down: CoreAudio switches/removes devices while the
370	        // machine heads into sleep, and the resulting config-change notifications
371	        // must not restart capture behind this intentional stop.
372	        sleeping = true
373	        sleepStartedAt = Date()
374	        // stopListening deliberately leaves `listeningIntent` alone: this is a
375	        // suspend, not "the counter was switched off", and the return path reads
376	        // that intent to decide whether to switch it back on.
377	        stopListening(reason: "system sleep")
378	    }

380	    @objc private func didWake() { systemDidReturn(reason: "system woke") }
381	    @objc private func screensDidWake() { systemDidReturn(reason: "displays woke") }
382	    @objc private func sessionDidBecomeActive() { systemDidReturn(reason: "session became active") }
383	    @objc private func screenDidUnlock() {
384	        // Distributed notifications are delivered on the main thread for an app
385	        // with a run loop, but say so explicitly rather than rely on it.
386	        DispatchQueue.main.async { [weak self] in self?.systemDidReturn(reason: "screen unlocked") }
387	    }

389	    /// One entry point for every "the machine is back" signal (wake from sleep or
390	    /// standby, displays waking, the session returning, the screen unlocking).
391	    /// Reactivates the counter **only if it was active before** — a Mac that was
392	    /// not listening when it went down comes back not listening.
393	    private func systemDidReturn(reason: String) {
394	        // These signals also fire with no sleep involved at all: the display
395	        // waking from the screensaver, a user switching back. Only a machine that
396	        // actually owes a resume reacts — restarting capture on every display wake
397	        // would rapid-cycle the mic (the wedge condition) for nothing.
398	        guard sleeping || (listeningIntent && !listening) else { return }
399	        if pendingResumeID != nil { return }   // the burst is one return, one resume
400	        // How long we were down, measured from willSleep. Nil means we never slept:
401	        // the signal is then a backstop over a start that failed earlier, and it
402	        // buys exactly one more attempt — not a fresh retry ladder.
403	        let asleep = sleepStartedAt.map { Date().timeIntervalSince($0) }
404	        // After a long standby the USB bus was powered down and devices come back
405	        // well after the wake notification, so settle for longer before re-acquiring.
406	        let standby = (asleep ?? 0) >= standbyThreshold
407	        let settle = standby ? standbySettleDelay : wakeSettleDelay
408	        let what = listeningIntent ? "resuming listening shortly"
409	                                   : "counter is \(offReason ?? "off"), staying off"
410	        if let asleep = asleep {
411	            AppLog.shared.log(String(format: "%@ after %.0fs %@ — %@", reason, asleep,
412	                                     standby ? "standby" : "sleep", what))
413	        } else {
414	            AppLog.shared.log("\(reason) while listening was down — \(what)")
415	        }
416	        resumeID &+= 1
417	        let id = resumeID
418	        pendingResumeID = id
419	        // Stay gated (`sleeping`) through the settle delay so wake-time device
420	        // re-enumeration can't trigger an early, un-settled restart; this resume is
421	        // the one entry point out of sleep. Capture the generation so a quick
422	        // re-sleep (lid closed again during the delay) aborts it — willSleep bumps
423	        // the generation, and this timer would otherwise fire immediately on the
424	        // *next* wake, un-gating and restarting un-settled.
425	        let generation = restartGeneration
426	        DispatchQueue.main.asyncAfter(deadline: .now() + settle) { [weak self] in
427	            guard let self = self, self.pendingResumeID == id else { return }
428	            self.pendingResumeID = nil
429	            guard generation == self.restartGeneration else {
430	                AppLog.shared.log("wake resume superseded by a later stop — skipping")
431	                return
432	            }
433	            self.sleeping = false          // always ungate, even when staying off,
434	            self.sleepStartedAt = nil      // or a manual start would stay blocked
435	            guard self.listeningIntent else {
436	                AppLog.shared.log("listening not resumed — counter is "
437	                    + "\(self.offReason ?? "off") (it was not active before sleep)")
438	                return
439	            }
440	            // A real return from sleep earns a fresh retry ladder; a backstop
441	            // signal (no sleep behind it) gets the single attempt below instead.
442	            if asleep != nil { self.startFailureStreak = 0 }
443	            self.requestListening()
444	            if self.speechAuthorized { self.voice.start() }   // idempotent
445	        }
446	    }

451	        if suppressConfigChange {
452	            configChangeSwallowed = true   // reconciled at settle time
453	            return

455	        AppLog.shared.log("audio configuration changed — reconfiguring")

605	    /// stays registered on the input device. Some USB webcam mics get wedged by
606	    /// that and go silent — no input registered in System Settings — until they're

608	    /// speech recogniser, which also holds the audio stream) deregisters the IOProc
609	    /// so the device is handed cleanly back to the system.

611	        sleeping = true          // gate any late config-change reaction during teardown

613	        // restarts (generation bump), stops speech, removes the tap, stops the
614	        // engine, and (via refreshTitle) drops the keep-awake assertion.

3	/// A tiny **operational** log — separate from `laughs.jsonl` — so that "the
4	/// service stopped" is self-diagnosing instead of invisible. It records lifecycle
5	/// events (started / stopped / slept / woke / reconfigured) and errors, one line
6	/// per event as `ISO8601␠␠LEVEL␠␠message`, to
7	/// `~/Library/Application Support/LaughCounter/laughcounter.log`.

9	/// Writes are serialised on a private queue and the file is rotated once when it
10	/// passes ~1 MB, so it can never grow without bound. Everything is also mirrored
11	/// to `NSLog` so it still shows up in Console.app.
12	final class AppLog {
13	    static let shared = AppLog()

15	    let fileURL: URL
16	    private let queue = DispatchQueue(label: "com.laughcounter.applog")
17	    private let maxBytes: UInt64 = 1_000_000
18	    private let iso: ISO8601DateFormatter = {
19	        let f = ISO8601DateFormatter()
20	        f.formatOptions = [.withInternetDateTime]

27	        let dir = base.appendingPathComponent("LaughCounter", isDirectory: true)

34	        let stamp = iso.string(from: Date())
35	        queue.async { [weak self] in

38	            self.rotateIfNeeded()
39	            if let handle = try? FileHandle(forWritingTo: self.fileURL) {
40	                defer { try? handle.close() }
41	                handle.seekToEndOfFile()
42	                handle.write(data)
43	            } else {
44	                try? data.write(to: self.fileURL)
45	            }
46	        }
47	    }

50	    /// keeping exactly one previous file. Called on the write queue.
51	    private func rotateIfNeeded() {
52	        guard let attrs = try? FileManager.default.attributesOfItem(atPath: fileURL.path),
53	              let size = attrs[.size] as? UInt64, size > maxBytes else { return }
54	        let rotated = fileURL.deletingPathExtension().appendingPathExtension("1.log")
55	        try? FileManager.default.removeItem(at: rotated)
56	        try? FileManager.default.moveItem(at: fileURL, to: rotated)

+// mic-probe.swift — a snapshot of what CoreAudio currently thinks of the input
+// device. Run it when the mic looks dead (see `diagnose-mic.sh`, which calls it).
+//
+// It queries the HAL directly rather than going through AVAudioEngine, because
+// HAL property reads are **not** TCC-gated: they report the truth even from a
+// Terminal that was never granted microphone access. The AVAudioEngine section
+// at the end *is* gated, and says so.
+//
+// The single most useful line it prints is `IsRunningSomewhere`. That is true
+// when some process still has an IOProc running on the device — which is
+// exactly the wedge state this project keeps chasing (a process that died with
+// its tap installed leaves the IOProc registered and the mic goes silent for
+// everyone until it is re-plugged). If the device is alive, has input channels,
+// and `IsRunningSomewhere` is true while LaughCounter is *not* listening,
+// something is holding the device that shouldn't be.

+// Usage:

+//   swift mic-probe.swift --capture   # additionally record ~3s and report peak

+                               mElement: kAudioObjectPropertyElementMain)

+               _ scope: AudioObjectPropertyScope = kAudioObjectPropertyScopeGlobal) -> UInt32? {
+    var addr = address(selector, scope)
+    var value: UInt32 = 0
+    var size = UInt32(MemoryLayout<UInt32>.size)
+    let err = AudioObjectGetPropertyData(object, &addr, 0, nil, &size, &value)
+    return err == noErr ? value : nil
+}
+
+func getFloat64(_ object: AudioObjectID, _ selector: AudioObjectPropertySelector,
+                _ scope: AudioObjectPropertyScope = kAudioObjectPropertyScopeGlobal) -> Float64? {
+    var addr = address(selector, scope)
+    var value: Float64 = 0
+    var size = UInt32(MemoryLayout<Float64>.size)
+    let err = AudioObjectGetPropertyData(object, &addr, 0, nil, &size, &value)
+    return err == noErr ? value : nil

+
+func getString(_ object: AudioObjectID, _ selector: AudioObjectPropertySelector) -> String? {
+    var addr = address(selector)
+    var value: CFString = "" as CFString
+    var size = UInt32(MemoryLayout<CFString>.size)
+    let err = withUnsafeMutablePointer(to: &value) { pointer -> OSStatus in
+        AudioObjectGetPropertyData(object, &addr, 0, nil, &size, pointer)
+    }
+    return err == noErr ? (value as String) : nil

+    // IsRunning: this process has IO running on it (always no here).
+    let running = getUInt32(device, kAudioDevicePropertyDeviceIsRunning)
+    let isDefault = device == defaultInput ? "  <== DEFAULT INPUT" : ""
+    print("\(name)\(isDefault)")
+    print("    id=\(device) uid=\(uid) transport=\(transport)")
+    print("    inputChannels=\(channels) nominalRate=\(Int(rate))Hz")
+    print("    IsAlive=\(yesNo(alive)) IsRunningSomewhere=\(yesNo(runningSomewhere)) "

+        var frames = 0

+            frames += Int(buffer.frameLength)

+            }

+        print("buffers=\(buffers) frames=\(frames) peak=\(String(format: "%.5f", peak))")

#!/bin/bash
#
# diagnose-mic.sh — collect everything needed to tell apart the three ways
# "the mic is dead after sleep" can happen. Run it on the Mac *while the
# symptom is present*, before quitting or relaunching LaughCounter (a relaunch
# destroys most of the evidence).
#
#   bash mac/scripts/diagnose-mic.sh              # read-only
#   bash mac/scripts/diagnose-mic.sh --capture    # also record ~3s (see below)
#
# It writes one report to /tmp/laughcounter-mic-diagnosis-<stamp>.txt and prints
# the path. The three states it separates:
#
#   1. App died         — crash report present, process gone or restarted. The
#                         tap's IOProc was abandoned, so the device is wedged
#                         for everyone until re-plugged.
#   2. App alive, stuck  — process is old and running, log shows failed starts
#                         or nothing at all since the wake. The mic is fine at
#                         the OS level; the app is not re-acquiring it.
#   3. App alive, silent — log says "listening started" after the wake and the
#                         engine is running, but no laughs are counted. The
#                         stream is running and delivering nothing.
#
# --capture opens the microphone from this script for three seconds, which
# needs the terminal to have microphone access. It is opt-in because it takes
# the device, and taking the device is the thing that can wedge it.

set -uo pipefail

STAMP="$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)"
OUT="/tmp/laughcounter-mic-diagnosis-${STAMP}.txt"
HERE="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
APP_LOG="$HOME/Library/Application Support/LaughCounter/laughcounter.log"

section() {
  {
    echo ""
    echo "================================================================"
    echo "== $1"
    echo "================================================================"
  } >>"$OUT"
}

exec 3>&1
{
  echo "LaughCounter mic diagnosis — $(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)"
  echo "host: $(sw_vers -productName) $(sw_vers -productVersion) ($(sw_vers -buildVersion))"
  echo "uptime: $(uptime)"
} >"$OUT"

# --- 1. Is the app running, and since when? -------------------------------
# An app whose start time is AFTER the last wake relaunched itself, which means
# it died. An app older than the sleep is state 2 or 3.
section "process"
PIDS="$(pgrep -x LaughCounter || true)"
if [ -z "$PIDS" ]; then
  echo "LaughCounter is NOT running" >>"$OUT"
else
  echo "pids: $PIDS" >>"$OUT"
  # shellcheck disable=SC2086
  ps -o pid,lstart,etime,%cpu,%mem,rss,state,command -p $PIDS >>"$OUT" 2>&1
fi
echo "" >>"$OUT"
echo "installed app bundle version:" >>"$OUT"
for APP in /Applications/LaughCounter.app "$HOME/Applications/LaughCounter.app"; do
  if [ -d "$APP" ]; then
    echo "  $APP  $(defaults read "$APP/Contents/Info" CFBundleShortVersionString 2>/dev/null) " \
         "($(defaults read "$APP/Contents/Info" CFBundleVersion 2>/dev/null))" >>"$OUT"
  fi
done

# --- 2. Did it crash? -----------------------------------------------------
# An uncatchable NSException aborts the process, applicationWillTerminate never
# runs, and the tap's IOProc is left registered on the device. If anything shows
# up here, that is the whole story.
section "crash reports (last 10)"
find "$HOME/Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports" /Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports \
     -maxdepth 1 -iname 'LaughCounter*' -print0 2>/dev/null \
  | xargs -0 ls -lt 2>/dev/null | head -10 >>"$OUT"
NEWEST_CRASH="$(find "$HOME/Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports" /Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports \
     -maxdepth 1 -iname 'LaughCounter*' -print0 2>/dev/null \
  | xargs -0 ls -t 2>/dev/null | head -1)"
if [ -n "$NEWEST_CRASH" ]; then
  echo "" >>"$OUT"
  echo "--- head of newest crash report: $NEWEST_CRASH ---" >>"$OUT"
  head -80 "$NEWEST_CRASH" >>"$OUT" 2>&1
  echo "" >>"$OUT"
  echo "--- exception / termination lines ---" >>"$OUT"
  grep -iE 'exception|termination|abort|required condition|signal' "$NEWEST_CRASH" \
    | head -30 >>"$OUT" 2>&1
else
  echo "(no LaughCounter crash reports found)" >>"$OUT"
fi

# --- 3. The app's own account of the sleep/wake ---------------------------
section "app activity log (last 150 lines)"
if [ -f "$APP_LOG" ]; then
  echo "path: $APP_LOG" >>"$OUT"
  echo "size: $(stat -f%z "$APP_LOG") bytes, last modified $(stat -f%Sm "$APP_LOG")" >>"$OUT"
  echo "" >>"$OUT"
  tail -150 "$APP_LOG" >>"$OUT"
else
  echo "no activity log at $APP_LOG" >>"$OUT"
fi

# --- 4. Sleep/wake history ------------------------------------------------
# Lines up the app log against what the machine actually did: which wake it
# was, how long the sleep lasted, and whether it was a dark wake.
section "power management sleep/wake history (last 60 events)"
pmset -g log 2>/dev/null \
  | grep -E 'Sleep  |Wake  |DarkWake|Notification' \
  | tail -60 >>"$OUT"

section "current power assertions"
pmset -g assertions >>"$OUT" 2>&1

# --- 5. What CoreAudio thinks ---------------------------------------------
section "CoreAudio HAL probe"
if command -v swift >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  if [ "${1:-}" = "--capture" ]; then
    swift "$HERE/mic-probe.swift" --capture >>"$OUT" 2>&1
  else
    swift "$HERE/mic-probe.swift" >>"$OUT" 2>&1
  fi
else
  echo "swift not found — install the Xcode command line tools (xcode-select --install)" >>"$OUT"
fi

section "system_profiler audio input devices"
system_profiler SPAudioDataType 2>/dev/null >>"$OUT"

section "coreaudiod"
ps -o pid,lstart,etime,%cpu,command -p "$(pgrep -x coreaudiod | head -1)" >>"$OUT" 2>&1

# --- 6. Unified log around the wake ---------------------------------------
# NSLog from the app plus whatever coreaudiod said. The app's own log misses
# anything that happened after an abort; this does not.
section "unified log: LaughCounter (last 3h)"
log show --last 3h --style compact \
  --predicate 'process == "LaughCounter" OR eventMessage CONTAINS "LaughCounter"' \
  2>/dev/null | tail -200 >>"$OUT"

section "unified log: coreaudiod errors/faults (last 3h)"
log show --last 3h --style compact --predicate \
  'process == "coreaudiod" AND (messageType == error OR messageType == fault)' \
  2>/dev/null | tail -150 >>"$OUT"

section "unified log: device add/remove around the wake (last 3h)"
log show --last 3h --style compact --predicate \
  '(subsystem == "com.apple.coreaudio") AND (eventMessage CONTAINS[c] "device" OR eventMessage CONTAINS[c] "IOProc")' \
  2>/dev/null | tail -150 >>"$OUT"

echo "" >&3
echo "Report written to: $OUT" >&3
echo "" >&3
echo "Summary:" >&3
{
  if [ -z "$PIDS" ]; then
    echo "  process: NOT RUNNING"
  else
    echo "  process: running (pid $PIDS), started $(ps -o lstart= -p "${PIDS%% *}" | xargs)"
  fi
  if [ -n "$NEWEST_CRASH" ]; then
    echo "  crash reports: present, newest $(basename "$NEWEST_CRASH")"
  else
    echo "  crash reports: none"
  fi
  if [ -f "$APP_LOG" ]; then
    echo "  last app log line: $(tail -1 "$APP_LOG")"
  fi
} >&3
echo "" >&3
echo "Send that file back (it contains no audio and no laugh data)." >&3

     -maxdepth 1 -iname 'LaughCounter*' -print0 2>/dev/null \

  head -80 "$NEWEST_CRASH" >>"$OUT" 2>&1

input.body:
"The mic is dead after sleep" has recurred across #22, #59, #61, #76 — and each round has been diagnosed after the evidence was already gone. From the menu bar the symptom looks identical in three cases that need completely different fixes:

1. **The app died** with its tap installed — the CoreAudio IOProc is abandoned and the device is wedged system-wide until re-plugged.
2. **The app is alive but never re-acquired the device** — the mic is fine at the OS level, the app just isn't starting.
3. **The app is alive with a running engine that delivers nothing** — the menu says "listening" and no buffers arrive. Nothing in the app currently detects this.

## What this adds

**`mac/scripts/diagnose-mic.sh`** — collects the whole picture in one pass while the symptom is present, into a single pasteable report:

- process start time (a start time *after* the wake means it died and relaunched)
- crash reports plus their exception/termination lines
- the app's activity log
- `pmset -g log` sleep/wake history, to line the app log up against what the machine actually did
- CoreAudio HAL state (via the probe below) and `system_profiler` audio devices
- unified log for `LaughCounter` and for `coreaudiod` errors/faults — which survives an abort, unlike the app's own log

**`mac/scripts/mic-probe.swift`** — the CoreAudio half. It reads the HAL directly rather than going through `AVAudioEngine`, because HAL property reads are **not** TCC-gated: it reports the truth even from a terminal that was never granted microphone access.

Its key output is `IsRunningSomewhere`. True while LaughCounter is *not* listening means some process still has IO running on the device — that is the wedge state, stated as a fact rather than inferred from the mic being silent. It also prints the `inputFormat`/`outputFormat` pair that `AudioHub.validatedFormat()` gates on, so "the app thinks the mic is gone" can be told apart from "the mic is gone".

The capture test is opt-in behind `--capture`, since taking the device is the thing that can wedge it, and it removes the tap and stops the engine on every exit path.

## Testing

`bash -n` clean. Neither script is reachable from the app or the build — they are operator tools, run by hand on the Mac exhibiting the symptom. The Swift probe has not been compiled (no macOS in this environment); it is written against documented CoreAudio property selectors and will be verified on the first real run.

## Notes

No fix yet — this is the instrument. Per `dev/procedures/mac-audio-lifecycle.md`, compile-green is not a gate for this area, and shipping another speculative `AudioHub` change without knowing which of the three states occurred is how the last two crash-on-launch builds happened.

content.text:
Those two answers together are the most informative combination possible, and they rule out the cause every previous round assumed.

**The app was alive and said "listening" — so this was not a crash.** #22/#61's mechanism was "process aborts, `applicationWillTerminate` never runs, IOProc left registered." That can't be it: the process was there. But the device was wedged system-wide anyway, which means **a live LaughCounter wedged it** — the app is the thing holding the device, not a corpse.

That points at one specific piece of code. `scheduleStartRetry` retries forever at a 60s ceiling, and `AppDelegate.swift:282` justifies that with "a start attempt is now a cheap format read that throws before touching the tap." **That comment is wrong.** The path is:

`requestListening()` → `audio.stop()` → +0.4s → `finishListening()` → `prepareFormat()` → `renewEngine()` → stop the old engine, **construct a new `AVAudioEngine`, touch `inputNode` (which instantiates the AUHAL unit and opens the device), `prepare()` (allocates its render resources)** → *only then* `validatedFormat()` throws → `audio.stop()`, engine dropped.

So every retry opens and tears down the input device and discards an engine. Once a minute, for as long as the mic is missing — 28 cycles across the display-sleep outage you measured, unbounded after a standby where the USB bus is slow to come back. Rapid-cycling a USB mic is the documented wedge condition; this is a slow version of it, running unattended for as long as it takes. Then a later cycle "succeeds" on a device the churn has already killed, `engine.start()` returns without error, and the menu says listening.

Which exposes the second, independent gap: **`listening` means `engine.start()` returned, not that audio is arriving.** Nothing in the app checks that buffers keep coming, so the menu bar cannot tell "listening" from "holding a dead device." That's why it lied to you — and it's true regardless of what caused the wedge.

The report will confirm or kill this in one look. My prediction, if I'm right:

- `IsRunningSomewhere=YES` on the input device, with LaughCounter alive and old (started before the sleep)
- a long run of `start failed — retrying in 60s` / `input device still unavailable` lines in the activity log after the wake
- then a `listening started` line — after which nothing was ever counted
- no crash report at all

If instead the log shows a clean `listening started` right after the wake with no retry churn before it, the cycling theory is dead and the cause is elsewhere.

> ⚠️ **Waiting on the diagnostic report before I change `AudioHub`.** `dev/procedures/mac-audio-lifecycle.md` is explicit that compile-green is not a gate here and that two crash-on-launch builds already shipped past CI on speculation — so I'd rather spend one run of the script than ship a third. Run `bash mac/scripts/diagnose-mic.sh` next time it's dead (before relaunching) and paste the report; the fix is two changes — probe the HAL cheaply instead of building an engine to find out the mic is missing, and add a buffer-liveness watchdog so "listening" has to mean audio is actually flowing.
